```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)

library(AlphaSimR)
```

## Introduction

Selection is how a simulated breeding program makes progress. Every
selection function in `AlphaSimR` answers the same three questions: which
individuals are candidates, what value they are ranked on, and how many
are kept. This article works through those questions, starting with
selection of individuals, then the use of family structure, then
selection on several traits at once, and ends with tools for predicting
what selection will achieve.

Two related topics have articles of their own. Selection on genomic
predictions is covered in `vignette("GenomicSelection")`, and selection
that limits the loss of genetic diversity is covered in the
[Optimal Contribution Selection](OptimalContributionSelection.html)
article.

## Setting up an example

The example population carries two traits with a negative genetic
correlation, as is common between a yield trait and a quality trait.
Phenotypes are generated automatically for every new population, because
the error variances are set.

```{r}
set.seed(1936)

founderPop = quickHaplo(nInd = 100, nChr = 10, segSites = 100)

SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
```
```{r include=FALSE}
SP$nThreads = 1L
```
```{r}
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 50, mean = c(0, 0), var = c(1, 1),
             corA = matrix(c(1, -0.3, -0.3, 1), nrow = 2))
SP$setVarE(h2 = c(0.3, 0.5))

basePop = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SP)
pop = randCross(basePop, nCrosses = 100, nProgeny = 10, simParam = SP)
nInd(pop)
```

`quickHaplo` is a reasonable choice here. Nothing in this article depends
on markers tracking QTL, which is where `quickHaplo` founders fall short
(see `vignette("GenomicSelection")`).

## What to select on

The `use` argument chooses the value that candidates are ranked on.

| `use` | Ranks on | Realistic? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `"pheno"` | phenotypes, the default | yes |
| `"ebv"` | estimated breeding values in the `ebv` slot | yes |
| `"gv"` | true genetic values | no, a diagnostic |
| `"bv"` | true breeding values, computed in `pop` | no, a diagnostic |
| `"rand"` | nothing; selection is at random | a control |

Phenotypes and estimated breeding values are what a breeder actually
sees. Genetic values and breeding values are known only in a simulation,
which makes them useful for asking how well a scheme could do if
evaluation were perfect. Random selection gives a baseline with no
selection at all, so a gain that also appears under `"rand"` is not
caused by selection.

```{r}
nSel = 100

compare = sapply(c("pheno", "gv", "bv", "rand"), function(u){
  selected = selectInd(pop, nInd = nSel, use = u, simParam = SP)
  meanG(selected) - meanG(pop)
})
rownames(compare) = c("Trait1", "Trait2")
round(compare, 3)
```

The columns are the genetic superiority of the selected individuals over
the whole population for each trait, the selection differential measured
on genetic values. Selection on trait 1 also moves trait 2, in the
opposite direction, because the traits are negatively correlated.
Selection on genetic values does best, phenotypic selection achieves
about half as much at a heritability of 0.3, and random selection
achieves nothing beyond sampling noise. The `"gv"` and `"bv"` columns are
identical because the traits are purely additive; with dominance they
would rank individuals differently.

### A criterion of your own

`use` can also be a function. It is called as `use(pop, trait, ...)` and
must return one value per individual. As an example, stabilizing
selection toward an intermediate optimum ranks individuals by how close
their phenotype is to a target, so the most extreme individuals are
discarded in both directions:

```{r}
nearTarget = function(pop, trait, target){
  -abs(pheno(pop)[, trait] - target)
}

stabilized = selectInd(pop, nInd = nSel, use = nearTarget, target = 0,
                       simParam = SP)
range(pheno(pop)[, 1])
range(pheno(stabilized)[, 1])
```

Arguments the function needs, such as `target` here, are passed through
`...` of the selection function.

## Selecting individuals

`selectInd` ranks every candidate and keeps the best `nInd`. A few
arguments change what "best" and "candidate" mean:

- `selectTop = FALSE` keeps the lowest values instead, for traits where
  smaller is better.
- `candidates` restricts selection to a subset, given by position or by
  ID, without having to subset the population first.
- `sex` selects only females (`"F"`) or males (`"M"`) when the
  simulation has separate sexes.
- `returnPop = FALSE` returns the positions of the selected individuals
  rather than a population, which is useful when the selected
  individuals have to be found in other objects, as below.

```{r}
# The ten lowest, from the first 500 individuals only
lowest = selectInd(pop, nInd = 10, selectTop = FALSE, candidates = 1:500,
                   returnPop = FALSE, simParam = SP)
lowest
```

When fewer candidates are available than requested, the default is to
warn and return all of them. `onShortfall = "error"` stops instead, which
is the safer choice inside a long simulation, and `onShortfall = "none"`
returns them silently.

```{r}
small = selectInd(pop[1:5], nInd = 10, onShortfall = "none", simParam = SP)
nInd(small)
```

`attrition` is the opposite of selection: it removes individuals at
random, each with probability `p`, to model losses that have nothing to
do with merit, such as plants that fail to establish.

```{r}
survivors = attrition(pop, p = 0.05)
nInd(survivors)
```

## Using family structure

Most breeding populations are made of families, and selection can take
that structure into account. Full-sib families are identified by their
mother and father.

```{r}
families = paste(pop@mother, pop@father)
length(unique(families))
```

- `selectFam` ranks families by the mean value of their members and keeps
  every member of the best `nFam` families.
- `selectWithinFam` keeps the best `nInd` individuals from every family.

```{r}
topFamilies = selectFam(pop, nFam = 10, simParam = SP)
nInd(topFamilies)

bestOfEach = selectWithinFam(pop, nInd = 1, simParam = SP)
nInd(bestOfEach)
```

`famType` chooses what counts as a family: `"B"` (the default) for full
sibs, or `"F"` and `"M"` for half sibs sharing a mother or a father.
An individual with an unknown parent is a family of its own.

### Why family structure matters

Truncation selection on phenotype favors whole families, because members
of a good family share good alleles. Over several generations that
concentrates the population on fewer families and erodes genetic
variance faster [@robertson1961Inbreeding]. Selecting within families first, and then across them,
caps how many individuals any one family contributes.

The comparison below runs three strategies for 15 generations from the
same population. Each keeps 20 parents a generation and makes 20 full-sib
families of 10:

- **truncation**: the best 20 individuals, regardless of family;
- **within family**: the best individual from each of the 20 families;
- **two-stage**: the best two from each family, then the best 20 of
  those, so that no family supplies more than two parents.

```{r}
startPop = randCross(basePop, nCrosses = 20, nProgeny = 10, simParam = SP)

runStrategy = function(strategy, nGen = 15){
  pop = startPop
  out = data.frame(generation = 0, meanG = meanG(pop)[1],
                   genicVarA = genicVarA(pop, simParam = SP)[1],
                   nFamilies = NA)
  for(gen in seq_len(nGen)){
    parents = switch(strategy,
      truncation = selectInd(pop, nInd = 20, simParam = SP),
      within = selectWithinFam(pop, nInd = 1, simParam = SP),
      twoStage = selectInd(selectWithinFam(pop, nInd = 2, simParam = SP),
                           nInd = 20, simParam = SP))
    nFamilies = length(unique(paste(parents@mother, parents@father)))
    pop = randCross(parents, nCrosses = 20, nProgeny = 10, simParam = SP)
    out = rbind(out, data.frame(generation = gen, meanG = meanG(pop)[1],
                                genicVarA = genicVarA(pop, simParam = SP)[1],
                                nFamilies = nFamilies))
  }
  out
}

strategies = c("truncation", "within", "twoStage")
results = lapply(strategies, runStrategy)
names(results) = strategies
```

```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
cols = c("black", "red", "blue")
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 15), ylim = range(sapply(results, `[[`, "meanG")),
     xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Mean genetic value")
for(i in seq_along(results)){
  lines(results[[i]]$generation, results[[i]]$meanG, col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topleft", legend = strategies, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 15), ylim = range(sapply(results, `[[`, "genicVarA")),
     xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Genic additive variance")
for(i in seq_along(results)){
  lines(results[[i]]$generation, results[[i]]$genicVarA, col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
}
```

```{r}
# Families contributing parents, averaged over the generations,
# and the state of the population after the last generation
round(sapply(results, function(x){
  c(nFamilies = mean(x$nFamilies, na.rm = TRUE),
    meanG = x$meanG[nrow(x)],
    genicVarA = x$genicVarA[nrow(x)])
}), 3)
```

In this run truncation selection gave the most gain over 15 generations,
but it drew its parents from about 12 of the 20 families on average and
lost the most genic variance. Selecting the best individual of every
family kept all 20 families and the most variance, at the cost of the
least gain, because it ignores the information in family means
altogether. The two-stage scheme falls between the two. Which balance is
right depends on the time horizon: variance lost now is gain that cannot
be made later, and over a longer horizon than this one the ranking of
the strategies can change.

Genic variance is used here rather than genetic variance because it
depends only on allele frequencies, so it measures diversity that has
been lost for good. Genetic variance also falls with the negative
linkage disequilibrium that selection creates, and that part is
recovered when selection stops (see the
[Quantitative Genetics](QuanGen.html) article).

A single simulation is one realization. A real comparison repeats each
strategy many times and compares the averages.

## Selecting and crossing in one step

Two functions combine selection with mating.

`selectCross` selects parents and crosses them at random. It is
`selectInd` followed by `randCross`, and takes `nInd`, or `nFemale` and
`nMale` when the simulation has separate sexes:

```{r}
progeny = selectCross(pop, nInd = 50, nCrosses = 100, nProgeny = 5,
                      simParam = SP)
nInd(progeny)
```

`selectOP` models open pollination: each selected plant produces
`nSeeds` seeds, a proportion `probSelf` of them by selfing and the rest
pollinated at random by the population. With `pollenControl = TRUE`,
only the selected plants contribute pollen, as when selection happens
before flowering.

```{r}
seeds = selectOP(pop, nInd = 50, nSeeds = 10, probSelf = 0.1,
                 simParam = SP)
nInd(seeds)
```

## Selecting on several traits

The `trait` argument usually names one trait, by number or by name, but
it can also be a function that combines the traits into a single value.
`selIndex` is such a function: given a matrix of values with one column
per trait and a vector of weights `b`, it returns the weighted sum.

What weights to use is the question of index selection. The Smith-Hazel
index [@smith1936Discriminant; @hazel1943Genetic] chooses the weights
that maximize the response in an aggregate genotype, the sum of the
genetic values weighted by their economic values. `smithHazel` computes
them from the economic weights and the genetic and phenotypic
covariance matrices:

```{r}
econWt = c(1, 1)
b = smithHazel(econWt, varG(pop), varP(pop))
b
```

The index puts less weight on the less heritable trait than the economic
weights alone would. Selecting on it, and comparing with selection on
each trait alone:

```{r}
superiority = function(selected){
  delta = meanG(selected) - meanG(pop)
  c(delta, aggregate = sum(econWt * delta))
}

round(rbind(
  trait1 = superiority(selectInd(pop, nSel, trait = 1, simParam = SP)),
  trait2 = superiority(selectInd(pop, nSel, trait = 2, simParam = SP)),
  index = superiority(selectInd(pop, nSel, trait = selIndex, b = b,
                                simParam = SP))
), 3)
```

Selecting on either trait alone improves that trait at the expense of
the other. The index gives up some of each trait's individual response
and in exchange gives the largest improvement in the aggregate genotype,
which is what it is designed to maximize.

`selIndex` is applied to whatever `use` names, so the same weights can be
applied to estimated breeding values with `use = "ebv"`. Weights for
EBVs are not the Smith-Hazel weights for phenotypes; with EBVs from a
multiple trait model, the economic weights themselves are the usual
choice.

## Predicting the response

The breeder's equation predicts the response to truncation selection in
one generation as $R = i h^2 \sigma_P$, where $i$ is the selection
intensity, the mean of the selected individuals in standard deviations
of the criterion [@falconer1996Introduction]. `selInt` gives $i$ for a
proportion selected, assuming a normal distribution and an infinite
population:

```{r}
p = nSel / nInd(pop)
selInt(p)
```

The prediction can be checked against the simulation. The breeding
values of the parents are computed in the population they were selected
from, the reference population in which they are defined, so the
selected individuals are found with `returnPop = FALSE`:

```{r}
h2 = varA(pop)[1, 1] / varP(pop)[1, 1]
predicted = selInt(p) * h2 * sqrt(varP(pop)[1, 1])

take = selectInd(pop, nInd = nSel, returnPop = FALSE, simParam = SP)
bvPop = bv(pop, simParam = SP)[, 1]
selectionResponse = mean(bvPop[take]) - mean(bvPop)

offspring = randCross(pop[take], nCrosses = 500, nProgeny = 2,
                      simParam = SP)
realized = meanG(offspring)[1] - meanG(pop)[1]

round(c(predicted = predicted, parentsBV = selectionResponse,
        offspring = unname(realized)), 3)
```

The three values agree closely. The predicted response assumes an
infinite population and normally distributed phenotypes, and the mean
breeding value of the selected parents is what the prediction actually
targets. The offspring mean differs from it only by Mendelian sampling
in a finite number of offspring, since for an additive trait the
expected value of an offspring is the mean of its parents' breeding
values. The equation describes one generation; over several, selection
reduces the genetic variance through the Bulmer effect
[@bulmer1971Effect] and the response per generation falls.

`usefulness` summarizes a population by the mean value of its best
individuals, the top proportion `p`, a measure used to choose among
crosses by the expected value of their best progeny
[@zhong2007Using]. It is a quick way to rank several
candidate populations by what selection within each could deliver, using
genetic values by default:

```{r}
usefulness(pop, p = 0.1, simParam = SP)
```

## Selecting among populations

When a simulation holds several populations together in a `MultiPop`,
such as one per family or per breeding program, `selectPop` keeps the
best `nPop` of them, ranked on a summary (`mean` by default) of the
values named by `use` and `trait`, and `calcPopValue` computes such a
summary for every population. The other selection functions also accept
a `MultiPop`, and select within each of its populations.
